prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Cloudflare, Inc." (ticker NET). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Cloudflare fits Rule Breaker investing closely: it leads the emerging edge-network and AI-agent infrastructure market, has a founder CEO with a clear vision, strong momentum (from $177 at end-January 2026 to $296 in mid-October) and is widely called overvalued. Its main gaps are a brand ordinary consumers rarely notice and recent outages.
summaries.buffett: Cloudflare has a durable network advantage, but it does not fit Buffett's approach well: it has never earned a GAAP profit, return on capital is negative, results depend on continued heavy investment, and at about 42 times trailing sales there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would appreciate the scale-economics and network-effect moat and the founder-led culture, but the business is still unprofitable on a GAAP basis, dilutes shareholders through stock pay, and trades at a price that assumes many years of flawless growth.
summaries.lynch: Cloudflare is a clear fast grower (revenue up 36% in Q2 2026) with an easy story, but Lynch's PEG test fails badly: a forward non-GAAP P/E of about 235 against roughly 33-36% EPS growth, and it is anything but overlooked by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: Cloudflare scores well on Fisher's growth points: a long sales runway, a steady stream of new products from R&D, strong sales execution (large customers up 27%) and long-term-minded management. Weak profit margins and recent gross-margin erosion are the main shortfalls.
summaries.graham: Cloudflare fails nearly every Graham defensive criterion: it has no record of GAAP profits, pays no dividend, and trades at a multiple of earnings and book value far above Graham's limits, so it is not a candidate for a defensive investor.
summaries.thiel: Cloudflare answers most of Thiel's questions well: a near-monopoly position as the reverse proxy for 85.8% of proxied websites, a founder-led team, a free-tier distribution engine and a durable network. Whether its technology is ten times better than AWS or Akamai at large enterprises is less clear.
summaries.gerstner: Cloudflare is a leading beneficiary of the AI-agent and cloud trend, with accelerating revenue growth and improving free cash flow, and it 'got fit' with a 20% workforce cut in 2026. At roughly 40 times sales and about 235 times forward non-GAAP earnings, the valuation leaves little room for error.
summaries.druckenmiller: The business looks set to improve over the next 18-24 months as revenue growth re-accelerated to 36% and estimates rose, and AI traffic is a clear catalyst. However, the stock fell about 15% from its September high as AI-financing worries hit high-multiple software, so liquidity and sentiment are a real risk.
summaries.smith: Cloudflare has a high gross margin and a strong moat, but Terry Smith's tests of high return on capital and strong cash conversion of profits are not yet met, as GAAP operating income is negative, and the free-cash-flow yield of about 0.3% means investors would be overpaying by his standards.
summaries.greenblatt: Cloudflare scores at the bottom of the Magic Formula: GAAP operating profit is negative, so both earnings yield and return on capital are negative.
summaries.akre: Cloudflare has two legs of Akre's stool, a strong business with a long reinvestment runway and talented founder management, but its returns on capital are not yet high or proven, and the share price is far from reasonable.
summaries.pabrai: Cloudflare is not a Dhandho bet: it is a well-known, richly priced growth stock with no margin of safety, and the downside if growth slows from a ~40x sales multiple could be large, even though permanent business failure is unlikely.
summaries.wood: Cloudflare fits ARK's disruptive-innovation lens as an infrastructure layer for AI inference, AI agents and cloud networking whose unit costs fall with scale, with an addressable market that could expand sharply as non-human traffic grows.
summaries.ackman: Cloudflare has a dominant, hard-to-replicate network and long growth runway, but it is not the simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business at a reasonable price that Pershing Square looks for.
summaries.sleep: Cloudflare shares some 'scale economics shared' traits, offering free plans and egress-free storage and passing scale savings back to customers, and its founder runs it for the long term; Nick Sleep would likely be uneasy about the stock-based dilution and the very high valuation.
summaries.valentine: Cloudflare is a textbook Valentine company: it solved a big, painful problem (protecting and speeding up websites) for an enormous market, with technology that was hard to build and a founder team still in charge 17 years later.
summaries.nash: Cloudflare scores well on Nash's growth, secular-trend and quality categories (revenue +36%, Rule of 40 passed, founder CEO, cash above debt) but fails his instant-kill test on operating margin (GAAP -9.6% in FY2025) and his DCF and PEG valuation checks badly at about $296 a share.

momentum.evidence: The stock rose from a $177.35 month-end close in January 2026 to $296.12 on October 16, 2026 (about +67%), even after falling from $347.28 at end-September.

g4.evidence: Co-founders Matthew Prince (CEO since 2009) and Michelle Zatlyn still lead the company, which was backed early by venture firms such as Union Square Ventures, NEA and Venrock and is about 83% owned by institutions.

g6.evidence: Commentators routinely call Cloudflare overvalued; it trades around 40 times trailing sales and the lowest analyst target in October 2026 was $160, about 46% below the price.

simple.evidence: The core idea (a global network that speeds up and protects websites) is simple, but the many products (Zero Trust, Workers, AI inference) and the still-maturing business make it harder for a generalist to value.

b2.evidence: Revenue has grown every year from $431.1M in FY2020 to $2,167.9M in FY2025, but the company has never reported a full-year GAAP profit.

integrity.evidence: Management is unusually candid (detailed public outage post-mortems) and holds convertible debt rather than issuing equity often, but dual-class shares give founders control and stock compensation dilutes owners about 2% a year.

b6.evidence: Cloudflare builds almost all products in-house on its own network rather than doing large acquisitions, and charts its own course with free tiers and pay-per-crawl.

roic.evidence: GAAP operating income was -$207.2M in FY2025 and -$205.7M in Q2 2026 alone (including $150.7M of restructuring), so return on capital is negative.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was positive at $260.6M in FY2025 (12% of revenue) despite a GAAP net loss of $102.3M, but it depends heavily on adding back stock compensation.

b10.evidence: Reinvestment has grown revenue about fivefold from $431.1M (FY2020) to $2,167.9M (FY2025), and market value of roughly $105 billion far exceeds the capital retained.

safety.evidence: At $296.12 the market value is about $105 billion, roughly 42 times trailing revenue of $2,512M and over 300 times trailing free cash flow, so there is no margin of safety on conservative assumptions.

fairprice.evidence: Even for 30%+ growth, about 235 times 2026 non-GAAP EPS guidance of $1.25-1.26 and a 0.3% free-cash-flow yield is a demanding price.

mu5.evidence: The network and customer base are durable, but failure paths include hyperscaler bundling, major outages, AI-capex margin pressure and a valuation collapse if growth slows.

reinvest.evidence: Cloudflare can keep reinvesting in new products and network capacity across security, developer and AI markets, with revenue growth re-accelerating to 36% in Q2 2026.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear fast grower: the edge network that protects and speeds up the internet and now carries AI agent traffic.

ly3.evidence: Forward non-GAAP P/E of about 235 (on $1.26 EPS) is far above EPS growth of roughly 33-36%, and GAAP P/E is negative.

runway.evidence: Large customers grew 27% to 4,698, developers passed 7.4 million and new markets such as Zero Trust, AI inference and pay-per-crawl give many years of growth room.

ly7.evidence: Insiders sold about 458,839 shares (~$138M) in the last quarter, including Michelle Zatlyn's 33,003 shares at $348.29 on Oct 7, 2026, and diluted share count rose from 299.8M (FY2020) to 354.3M (Q2 2026).

ly8.evidence: Cloudflare is covered by over 30 analysts, is 83% institutionally owned and is a popular AI-infrastructure stock.

fi2.evidence: Cloudflare launches dozens of products a year through its Innovation Weeks, moving from CDN into Zero Trust, Workers, R2, Workers AI and pay-per-crawl.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $512.5M in FY2025 has produced new revenue lines such as Cloudflare One and the developer platform, helping revenue grow about 30% a year.

fi4.evidence: Its free-tier funnel plus enterprise sales added 986 large customers in the 12 months to June 2026 and over 80,000 paying customers in Q2 2026, and Q4 2025 had its largest-ever contract.

longterm.evidence: Management keeps investing heavily in network, AI capacity and new products ahead of profits, as Prince has done since founding in 2009.

gr1.evidence: With about $105 billion market value and $2.5 billion trailing revenue it is a large company, though young and still unprofitable.

ni10.evidence: Cloudflare has reported a GAAP net loss every year, including -$102.3M in FY2025.

gr4.evidence: Cloudflare has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: GAAP EPS has been negative throughout its public history (-$0.29 in FY2025).

gr6.evidence: Average GAAP earnings are negative, so the price cannot be 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: GAAP P/E is negative and price to book is about 65 times ($105B market value vs $1,620M equity), far beyond Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Its all-services-on-every-server network gives a large cost and ease-of-use edge (free DDoS protection, 74.5% gross margin vs Akamai's 59%), but not a proven tenfold technical lead over AWS or Akamai.

timing.evidence: Non-human traffic passed half of Cloudflare's network traffic in Q2 2026 and revenue growth re-accelerated to 36%, showing AI agents are driving demand now.

th3.evidence: It started with free protection for small websites, won a dominant share of that niche (85.8% of reverse-proxied sites) and expanded into enterprise security, networking and developer markets.

team.evidence: Co-founders Matthew Prince and Michelle Zatlyn have led the company since 2009, building it from a spam-tracking project into a $2.2 billion revenue business.

th5.evidence: Its free plan and self-serve sign-up feed a large pipeline that a growing enterprise and channel sales force (31% of Q2 2026 revenue via channel partners) converts into paying contracts.

durable.evidence: A global network in 335+ cities with deep peering and threat data is very hard to replicate, so its position should hold for 10-20 years, barring hyperscaler bundling.

th7.evidence: Its early bet that a single global network could run every security and compute service, and now its push to make AI crawlers pay publishers, were contrarian, but rivals now see the same opportunities.

trend.evidence: Cloudflare benefits from cloud adoption, cybersecurity spending and AI agents, describing itself as 'the platform they run on and the network they pass through'.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth accelerated from 30% in FY2025 to 34% in Q4 2025 and 36% in Q2 2026, and FY2026 guidance was raised from $2,785-2,795M to $2,864-2,870M.

dr2.evidence: Rising net retention (120%), RPO up 38% to $2.73B and a cost base cut by the 2026 restructuring point to better margins and growth in 18-24 months.

dr4.evidence: As a long-duration growth stock it benefits from lower rates, but the October 2026 sell-off over AI-financing worries shows sensitivity to liquidity and sentiment.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 2026 results (guided $736-737M), AI-agent traffic growth, pay-per-crawl monetization and margin gains from the workforce cut.

dr7.evidence: With ~235 times forward non-GAAP earnings, a recent 15% drawdown and GAAP losses, a large concentrated position would carry high valuation risk.

gm.evidence: GAAP gross margin was 74.5% in FY2025, though it has fallen from 77.3% in FY2024 to 71.8% in Q2 2026.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $314.9M against a roughly $105 billion market value is a yield of about 0.3%.

gb2.evidence: GAAP operating income is negative (-$207.2M in FY2025) against an enterprise value of about $104 billion.

pa2.evidence: There is no business setback; the business is growing 36%, and the recent share-price fall reflects sector sentiment rather than a fixable company problem.

pa4.evidence: Permanent business failure is unlikely given $4.16B of cash and investments and growing revenue, but buying at ~40 times sales risks a large, long-lasting loss if growth slows.

wo1.evidence: Cloudflare is a leading infrastructure provider for AI inference at the edge (Workers AI) and for managing AI crawler and agent traffic.

wo2.evidence: Spreading services over a shared global network lowers unit costs and lets it offer free tiers and egress-free storage, but gross margin has recently fallen as AI capacity costs rose.

wo3.evidence: It combines cloud computing, cybersecurity and AI, but not other ARK platforms such as robotics or energy storage.

wo4.evidence: AI-agent traffic and new markets could expand its market substantially, but its core security and networking markets are already large, making a many-times increase in five years uncertain.

ac3.evidence: As a subscription software and network business it has little exposure to commodity prices, though its valuation is sensitive to interest rates.

ns1.evidence: It passes scale savings to customers through free DDoS protection, free plans and no egress fees on R2, which makes it hard for smaller rivals to compete.

ns4.evidence: Continued growth in network reach, developers (7.4 million) and AI traffic suggests its position in 10-20 years should be stronger than today.

va2.evidence: It solves large, painful problems: cyberattacks, slow websites and insecure remote access for millions of organizations.

tn1.evidence: Cloudflare is built as internet infrastructure and now serves the AI-agent and inference trend directly, not a legacy business retrofitting.

tn2.evidence: Often seen as a CDN or security vendor, it is becoming a full 'connectivity cloud' and AI-agent platform, with non-human traffic now over half of its network.

tn3.evidence: It is a ~$105 billion US company founded in 2009, outside the small-cap, Chinese, commodity, airline, seasonal and startup zones.

tn4.evidence: It passes revenue growth (every year since FY2020) and more cash than debt ($4,162.8M vs $3,270.3M), with a valid miss on GAAP profit given positive free cash flow and a clear path to profit.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each of the last six quarters ($52.9M, $33.3M, ~$75.0M, $99.4M, $84.1M, $56.4M from Q1 2025 to Q2 2026), and cash and investments exceeded convertible debt throughout.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 29.8% in FY2025 and 36% in Q2 2026.

tn7.evidence: Q2 2026 revenue growth of 36% plus a trailing free-cash-flow margin of about 12.5% gives roughly 48, above 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 revenue rose 29.8% versus total operating expenses up 26.1%, but in the first half of 2026 expenses rose 40.9% (including $150.7M of restructuring) versus revenue up 34.7%.

tn9.evidence: It fails the operating-margin test (GAAP -9.6% in FY2025, non-GAAP about 14%), although market cap, cash versus debt, short interest (2.4%), growth, earnings beats and age (founded 2009) all pass.

tn10.evidence: There is no existential threat, but it faces regulatory pressure over content and piracy blocking, such as Italy's roughly €14 million AGCOM fine in January 2026.

tn11.evidence: Cloudflare provides a global network that helps businesses keep their websites, apps, staff and AI agents fast and secure, and charges subscriptions and usage fees; customers pick it for one integrated, low-cost platform.

tn13.evidence: Total 90: cash vs debt 5, revenue growth 10, operating margin 0, short interest 10 (2.4%), institutional ownership 10 (83%), revenue faster than expenses 10 (FY2025), 5-year return vs S&P 0 (not shown to beat), moat 10, CEO 10, pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture 5 (after 20% layoff), talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year and GAAP operating margin improved from -24.8% (FY2020) to -9.6% (FY2025), but free cash flow was negative in FY2020-FY2022 before turning positive and rising to $260.6M in FY2025.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage fails because GAAP operating income is negative, and assets excluding goodwill are only about 1.26 times liabilities, though the current ratio is 1.82 and liabilities are about 3.0 times equity.

tn18.evidence: Founder-CEO Matthew Prince has 17 years in the role and a strong growth and innovation record, but there are no open-market share purchases and GAAP margins remain negative.

tn20.evidence: Cloudflare beat non-GAAP EPS consensus in Q1 2026 ($0.25 vs $0.23) and Q2 2026 ($0.29 vs $0.27) and has a long record of revenue and EPS beats.

tn21.evidence: There is no fraud, auditor change or acquisition spree, but gross margins are declining and insiders sold about $138M of stock last quarter while the shares ran up.

tn22.evidence: It has $2.2 billion of revenue, positive free cash flow and funds itself mainly with convertible notes rather than repeated share sales.

tn24.evidence: At about $105 billion, 42 times trailing sales and a 0.3% FCF yield, the price implies decades of 25-30%+ growth with much higher margins, more than the current ~30-36% growth and 12% FCF margin deliver.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year averages of ~30.5% revenue growth (trimmed to 25%) and a ~10.4% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth and $893M net cash at a 12% discount rate gives roughly $21 per share, far below $296.12.

tn26.evidence: It passes the Rule of 40 (about 48), but at about 42 times trailing sales and a PEG near 7 (forward non-GAAP P/E ~235 vs ~33% EPS growth) it is not attractive.
